equation.name: Temperature a world glows at, with its own heat
equation.formula:
t4 = (1 - A) * S / (4 * sigma) + F / sigma
T = sqrt(sqrt(max(t4, 0)))

S.name: starlight arriving on each square metre

source.text: Pearl, J. C. and Conrath, B. J. 1991, J. Geophys. Res. 96, 18921

explain.curious: Everything glows by its own warmth. A world warmed only by its star glows at the bare-ball temperature; Jupiter, Saturn and Neptune glow warmer because they are still losing the heat they were born with.
explain.science: Global energy balance: absorbed starlight spread over the whole sphere plus internal heat flux, radiated as a black body. This is the effective temperature Voyager and Cassini measured for the giants (Neptune 59.3 K, Pearl and Conrath 1991). The same block gives a star its effective temperature when the internal flux is its own luminosity over its surface.

equation.name: How much starlight a world sends back
equation.formula: X = A * pi * R * R * (Rs / d) * (Rs / d)

X.name: reflected light as an area of the star's face

source.text: Williams, D. R., NASA Planetary Fact Sheets, NSSDCA

explain.curious: Planets shine mostly by borrowed light. How much comes back depends on how big the world is, how pale it is, and how much of its star's light reaches it.
explain.science: A sphere of radius R at distance d intercepts πR² of a flux that, for a star of radius R* glowing at T*, is π B_λ(T*) (R*/d)². A fraction A (the Bond albedo) is sent back. Written as an effective area so the reflected spectrum is that area times the star's surface brightness. Grey albedo: real albedos vary with wavelength.

params.description: proton number density at 1 au, per cm³ (Sun: about 7)
radial field at 1 au, nT (Sun: about 3.5)

Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press, chapter 9 (magnetopause stand-off from pressure balance, Chapman-Ferraro compression factor 2) https://www.cambridge.org/9780521457149

equation.name: The star's wind where the world is
equation.formula:
x = au / d
rho = n1 * per_cc * m_p * x * x
v = vk * km
omega = 2 * pi / (Pd * day)
B = Br * nT * x * x * omega * d / v

explain.curious: Stars blow a thin wind of charged gas that carries their magnetic field out past the planets, wound into a spiral by the star's spin like water from a garden sprinkler.
explain.science: Parker's wind at constant speed: density falls as 1/d², the radial field as 1/d², and the azimuthal field B_φ = B_r Ω d / v as 1/d. B_φ is the part of the field across the flow that a magnetosphere intercepts. Defaults are solar values at 1 au; a star's own wind comes with stellar activity (O10).

checks.says: magnetic moment must be zero or more, got {}

references: Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press, chapter 9 (magnetopause stand-off from pressure balance, Chapman-Ferraro compression factor 2) https://www.cambridge.org/9780521457149

equation.name: Where a world's magnetic field holds off the wind
equation.formula:
ram = rho * v * v
R = if M <= 0 or ram <= 0 then 0 else (mu0 * M * M / (8 * pi * pi * ram)) ^ (1/6)

M.name: strength of the world's magnet (dipole moment)

R.name: where the field holds the wind off

source.text: Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: A magnetic field holds the wind off like a bubble. Earth's bubble reaches about ten Earth radii towards the Sun; a world with no field has none.
explain.science: Pressure balance at the nose: the dipole field there, doubled by the currents on the boundary (Chapman-Ferraro), against the wind's ram pressure. Ignores plasma inside the bubble, which inflates Jupiter's to about twice this.

params.description: share of the intercepted magnetic power that comes out as radio (Zarka: about 2×10⁻³)

references: Zarka, P. 2007, Plasma interactions of exoplanets with their parent star and associated radio emissions, Planet. Space Sci. 55, 598: the radio-magnetic Bode's law, P_radio ≈ 2×10⁻³ of the incident magnetic power https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007P%26SS...55..598Z

Zarka, P., Treumann, R. A., Ryabov, B. P. and Ryabov, V. B. 2001, Magnetically-driven planetary radio emissions and application to extrasolar planets, Astrophys. Space Sci. 277, 293. doi:10.1023/A:1012221527425
atoms.shown: P = η (B_⊥² / μ₀) v π R_mp²  if R_mp > R, else 0

equation.name: Radio roar of a world's aurorae
equation.formula: P = if Rmp <= R then 0 else eta * B * B / mu0 * v * pi * Rmp * Rmp

Rmp.name: where the field holds the wind off

eta.name: share that comes out as radio

explain.curious: Magnetised planets are radio beacons. Jupiter is the loudest radio source in the sky after the Sun at long wavelengths; a world with no field is silent.
explain.science: The radio-magnetic Bode's law: every magnetised planet in the Solar System puts about the same small share of the wind's magnetic energy flux through its magnetosphere's cross-section into auroral radio. No magnetosphere (stand-off inside the body) gives no radio.

checks.says: magnetic moment must be zero or more, got {}

references: Treumann, R. A. 2006, The electron-cyclotron maser for astrophysical application, Astron. Astrophys. Rev. 13, 229: auroral radio is emitted near the local electron gyrofrequency f = eB/(2π m_e). doi:10.1007/s00159-006-0001-y

equation.name: Highest note of a world's radio aurorae
equation.formula:
B = mu0 * M / (2 * pi * R * R * R)
f = e / m_e * B / (2 * pi)

M.name: strength of the world's magnet (dipole moment)

f.name: highest radio frequency of its aurorae

source.text: Treumann, R. A. 2006, Astron. Astrophys. Rev. 13, 229

explain.curious: Auroral radio comes out at the rate electrons circle the field lines, so a stronger field means a higher top note. Jupiter's reaches tens of megahertz; Earth's only a few.
explain.science: Electron-cyclotron maser emission sits near the local gyrofrequency; its highest frequency is set by the strongest field, at the magnetic pole on the surface: B_pole = μ₀M / (2π R³) for a dipole. Real surface fields with multipoles go higher (Jupiter's 40 MHz cutoff).
